rightsReview: DOWNLOAD-ONLY pending a Catalog of Copyright Entries check — see packs/popeye-color/RIGHTS-REVIEW. The July 2026 field guide calls the Technicolor two-reelers a 'murkier claim'; the manifest basis below (IA PD marks + non-renewal) predates that. No takedown and no dispute on record — the gap is documentary. Not bundled in the App Store binary until the renewal volumes are read.
rightsNote: FILM COPYRIGHT: not renewed. Verified 2026-07-29 against CCE 3rd Series Parts 12-13 — Sindbad (1936) in 1963 Jul-Dec / 1964 both halves, Ali Baba (1937) in 1964 Jul-Dec / 1965 both halves, Aladdin (1939) in 1966 Jul-Dec / 1967 both halves — by OCR full-text search plus neighbourhood checks on the scans. The negative is substantive: United Artists Associated and United Artists Television were renewing the Popeye ONE-reelers throughout these same volumes (What, No Spinach?, MP6500 -> R316550, 31 May 1963; The Spinach Roadster in 1964; Scrap the Japs, L11702 -> R474660, 11 Dec 1969), and these three two-reel specials are not among them. This is the best published evidence short of a formal Copyright Office search report (Form 4). Every CCE renewal page carries the Office's own footer noting the printed entries alone may not reflect the complete record, and pre-1978 renewals are not in the online database. SEPARATE AND LIVE: non-renewal clears the FILM only. The Popeye CHARACTERS have their own live chain of title (King Features / Hearst, whose renewals DO appear in these same volumes) plus trademark rights. A distinct question, unresolved here, for counsel before publication. Play the films; keep Popeye out of dumbTV marketing, artwork and store copy. ALSO: only these three colour two-reelers are PD. The regular B&W Popeye shorts are NOT.

editorial.history: Fleischer's answer to Disney's move into features. Rather than a feature, Paramount let them make two-reel Technicolor specials at roughly triple the usual length and budget — and they used them to show off the studio's stereoptical process, a rotating three-dimensional miniature set placed behind the animation cels to give real depth on background pans. Nothing else in 1930s animation looks quite like it.
editorial.synopsis: The three colour two-reelers: Popeye Meets Sindbad the Sailor, Popeye Meets Ali Baba's Forty Thieves, and Aladdin and His Wonderful Lamp. These three are the only Popeye films in the public domain — the regular black-and-white shorts are not.
